clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, late-onset axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy caused by mutations in MPZ, the gene for myelin protein zero (P0), the most abundant protein of peripheral nervous system myelin.

MPZ is markedly pleiotropic: different mutations produce early-onset demyelinating CMT1B, late-onset axonal CMT2I/2J, dominant-intermediate CMT and Dejerine-Sottas or congenital hypomyelinating phenotypes.
CMT2I usually presents in later adulthood with distal weakness, sensory loss and sometimes prominent neuropathic pain.
The allelic subtype CMT2J is distinguished by sensorineural hearing loss and pupillary abnormalities such as a tonic (Adie-like) pupil.
Nerve conduction studies show axonal or borderline-intermediate features with only mild slowing, contrasting with the markedly slowed velocities of demyelinating CMT1B.
The position of the mutation within P0 broadly influences whether the phenotype is early demyelinating or late axonal.
Late-onset presentation and possible relapsing course can closely mimic chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
A careful pedigree, audiometry and pupillary examination help separate CMT2I from its allelic and non-allelic mimics.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2I is an autosomal dominant axonal neuropathy caused by heterozygous mutations in MPZ (chromosome 1), which encodes myelin protein zero (P0), a single-pass transmembrane immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion molecule that constitutes the majority of peripheral myelin protein. P0 mediates homophilic adhesion between adjacent myelin wraps and is essential for compaction and stability of the myelin sheath. The same gene gives rise to a wide phenotypic spectrum through distinct mechanisms: severe mutations that grossly disrupt myelin compaction cause early-onset demyelinating disease (CMT1B), whereas the milder, typically later-onset variants underlying CMT2I are thought to perturb axon-Schwann cell signalling and myelin maintenance, producing secondary axonal degeneration with relatively preserved conduction velocity. Allelic variants additionally impair cochlear and autonomic pupillary innervation, giving the CMT2J phenotype of deafness and tonic pupils. The genotype-phenotype correlation, in which mutation position and effect on P0 folding predict onset and electrophysiology, is a defining feature of MPZ-related disease.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1B (MPZ), the demyelinating counterpart of the same gene
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2J (MPZ) with deafness and pupillary abnormalities
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (MFN2), the commonest axonal CMT
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, which late-onset MPZ neuropathy can mimic
Other causes of late-onset axonal neuropathy such as paraproteinaemic or metabolic neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to document an axonal or intermediate pattern rather than uniform demyelination
Targeted MPZ sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel
Pure-tone audiometry to detect the sensorineural hearing loss of the allelic CMT2J phenotype
Formal pupillary examination for tonic (Adie-like) pupils
Three-generation pedigree to confirm dominant inheritance
Investigations to exclude acquired inflammatory or paraproteinaemic neuropathy when the course seems atypical
redFlags: A subacute or relapsing course with response to immunotherapy, suggesting a superimposed or alternative inflammatory neuropathy
Rapidly evolving deafness, visual or autonomic symptoms indicating the CMT2J end of the spectrum
Marked asymmetry or conduction block on studies, favouring an acquired demyelinating process
Prominent proximal or respiratory weakness that is unusual for this subtype
reference.prognosis: CMT2I is generally slowly progressive with onset in later life, and it is usually milder than the early-onset demyelinating MPZ phenotypes; most affected people remain ambulant, although neuropathic pain and, in the allelic CMT2J form, hearing loss add to morbidity.
pitfalls: Because MPZ is highly pleiotropic, a family history of demyelinating CMT does not exclude an axonal presentation in another relative carrying the same mutation.
Late-onset MPZ neuropathy is frequently misdiagnosed and treated as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
Failing to test for hearing loss and pupillary changes may cause the distinctive CMT2J features to be overlooked.
Interpreting only conduction velocity, without amplitudes and temporal dispersion, can miscategorise the neuropathy as purely demyelinating or purely axonal.
references: Peripheral and hereditary neuropathy reference texts
management: No disease-specific drug therapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Active neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents, as pain is often prominent in this subtype
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for distal weakness, sensory loss and foot drop
Audiology surveillance and hearing aids in the allelic CMT2J phenotype with sensorineural hearing loss
Ophthalmology review for tonic (Adie-like) pupil in the allelic CMT2J phenotype
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling and family screening
